title: Niche Construction
content_html:
Niche Construction

Niche construction is the evolutionary principle that organisms are not just shaped by environments - they also shape environments, and those modified niches feed back into evolution. Organisms actively modify their environments, changing the conditions of natural selection for themselves and other species. It’s not just adapting to an environment; it’s altering the environment itself in ways that feed back on evolution. Organisms change the environment → environment alters selection pressures → shapes future evolution. Modifications can persist across generations (ecological inheritance). So evolution is not only “genes → traits → fitness” but also “organisms → environment → selection.”

Everyday Examples

Earthworms: Restructure soil, oxygenating and fertilising it; future worms evolve within this new niche.
Beavers: Build dams, create ponds/wetlands; this changes predator/prey distributions, water flow, and even influences beaver morphology/behaviour.
Humans: Fire use (altered landscapes, food availability, cooking → gut/brain evolution), agriculture (fields, domesticated plants/animals, sedentary living → disease pressures, lactase persistence), technology (digital environments reshape cognition and social selection).

Evolution isn’t just about organisms passively adapting - they are also ecosystem engineers. Niche construction can accelerate or redirect evolution (e.g., dairying → lactase persistence within a few thousand years). Beyond genes, environments can carry information across generations (e.g., farmland, urban landscapes). This all makes evolution a reciprocal dance: genes adapt to environments, and environments adapt to organisms, and it blurs the boundary between biological and cultural evolution: humans especially build cognitive and cultural niches (language, institutions, technologies) that in turn select for new traits.

Select: Organisms select aspects of their environment to alter.
Change: The environment changes in response.
Reconstruct: Selection pressures are reconstructed for the next generation.
